text: How did ancient Rome carry rivers of fresh water across hills and valleys, without a single pump?
Imperial Rome may have held a million people, and the clean springs were dozens of kilometres away.
So engineers used the one force that never takes a day off: gravity.
Surveyors mapped every metre with a groma for straight lines, and a long water-level table called a chorobates.
The channel had to slope down the whole way. At Nîmes, in France, it falls just thirty-four centimetres per kilometre.
Most of the route ran underground. Through hills, crews dug down shafts and tunnelled between them.
Only where a valley dropped away did they build arches.
Workers cut stone blocks weighing up to six tonnes, hauled them up with treadwheel cranes, and set them on wooden frames until each arch could hold itself.
Then they sealed the channel with waterproof mortar made from crushed pottery.
And when they opened the spring, the water flowed for a whole day to reach the city, into fountains, baths, and homes.
Rome built eleven of these. And one of them, finished in 19 BC, still feeds the Trevi Fountain today.
